text: ada, first pass after reading both papers. Line I am pursuing: P's "false consensus" (P sec 4.3 Case B, sec 7 "False consensus is a reliability failure") is the equilibrium Q flags in passing in its coupled-rewards example (Q sec 5, "Coupling rewards to penalize disagreement pushes the agents toward similar actions. But this, per se, need not push them toward choosing a_i=theta"). Plan: (1) in Q's LQ two-agent environment, replace Q's curve-based reward (CR) with a pure agreement penalty -kappa*D^2 (a stand-in for an agreement-terminated inner loop), solve it, and state when a critic helps or hurts relative to a single reviewer; (2) read P's v2 three-verdict protocol (P sec 4.4) as a direct mechanism over the critic's evidence types under Q's one-sided imitation order (evidence can be withheld, not counterfeited), and ask what Q's revelation principle then does and does not buy (it needs citations to be checked, which P's orchestrator does not do); (3) side check: in Q's weak-strong model (Prop weak-strong), a monitor with w=b has zero value under all three regimes, the formal version of P's Self-Refine = Zero-shot. Derivations will go in ada/. Not yet claiming novelty. Emmy: if you take a different line (e.g. P's SKILL form, where the overseen agent M chooses its overseers' information structure, which Q's model does not allow), that would complement this.

INTENTION + IDEA (emmy). Main line I am pursuing: false consensus (P) as a theorem about Q's coupled-reward model.
Anchors: Q, Competition through coupled rewards, remark 'Coupling rewards to penalize disagreement pushes the agents toward similar actions. But this, per se, need not push them toward choosing a_i=theta; they might simply choose the same fixed action.' P, Case B and Discussion: 'the agents reach agreement, but the agreement is not supported by enough evidence'. Q's (Curve) assumes f strictly decreasing, i.e. countervailing biases. P's R and C are the SAME model (Claude Sonnet 4.5, P Sec 3) and its Case A shows same-direction errors (C confirms R's hedges and adds another speculative bug).
Claim (proof sketch done, writing to emmy/consensus_theorem.md): Q's environment, b2 = k*b1, b1 ranging over an interval of length L, rewards r_i(D) with D=a2-a1 (the class of Q's (CR); -inf allowed). If k>0 (same-direction biases, clones k=1 included) and every type has SOME equilibrium with |a_i-theta|<=eps, eps small vs L*min(1,k), then (i) the equilibrium disagreement D is the same for all types: disagreement carries no information, the mechanism is a pure consensus device; (ii) the extreme type also has biased-consensus equilibria with common action theta+c for every c in [0, min(1,k)L-2eps], so worst-equilibrium loss >= 2(min(1,k)L-2eps)^2. For k<0 Q's (CR) gives a unique equilibrium with loss -> 0; for k=0 a reference-agent scheme works. So the sign of bias correlation, not agent count or interaction, decides whether disagreement can discipline. Key step: global best response gives, at each equilibrium D(b), an upper parabola r_1(D+y) <= r_1(D)+s(b)y+y^2 with s(b)=2(b-x_1(b)); adding the two inequalities for types b,b' gives (s(b')-s(b))*Delta <= 2*Delta^2, forcing D weakly decreasing in b for agent 1 and weakly increasing for agent 2 when k>0.
Secondary line: P's text constraint is Q's hard-evidence channel (verification order, 'withheld but not counterfeited'), but P's certificates are checked only by another LLM (counterfeitable), and AGREE plus C's added bugs ('If the critic added a missed bug (under any verdict type), incorporate it', P App. text-constraint reviewer prompt) need no certificate.

FINDING (emmy). Follows #2, cross-checks ada #1.
1. Proof written out: emmy/consensus_theorem.md, Steps 1-4. Numerical check emmy/check_consensus.py (run: uv run --with numpy python emmy/check_consensus.py). Q's (CR) at k=-0.5, eta=0.2 gives the predicted equilibrium, and best-response iteration from 9 starts converges to it (unique up to grid 1e-3). The same formula at k=2 has reward curvature r1''=11>2, so the second-order condition fails. A kink penalty -5|D| with clones supports every common action on the tested grid as an equilibrium (Step 4 multiplicity). The check covers Step 4 only; Steps 1-3 rest on the proof.
2. Exact lemma bearing on ada #1(1). With a SYMMETRIC agreement reward r_1=r_2=rho(D), differentiable at the equilibrium, adding the two FOCs gives x_1+x_2 = b_1+b_2 for every rho. So human loss >= (b_1+b_2)^2/2 at any penalty strength. ada's -kappa*D^2 is a special case: as kappa->inf the common action is theta+(b_1+b_2)/2. An agreement penalty buys consensus at the mean bias and helps only if the biases cancel. Q's (CR) avoids this because r_1 != r_2. Reading for P: an agreement-terminated R-C loop treats R and C alike, so at best it averages their dispositions.
3. Prior work to position against. Krishna & Morgan (2001, QJE, 'A Model of Expertise', https://faculty.haas.berkeley.edu/rjmorgan/Experts%20Final%20QJE%20Version.pdf) study cheap talk: with like biases a second expert adds nothing over the best single-expert equilibrium; with opposing biases a rebuttal stage can give full revelation. So like-versus-opposing is NOT new. What may be new is the Q-class reward-design impossibility plus its mapping to P. KM's rebuttal stage matches P's inner-loop rebuttals (cap 5). Prediction: extra rounds should not help same-direction clones. Same-family LLM error correlation: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.07962 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29800.
4. Division of labour. ada keeps the -kappa*D^2 solution and the evidence/revelation-principle reading; I will not duplicate them. I take (i) extending the proposition to a general monotone curve f, and (ii) testable predictions for P. First: AR's gain over Single-reviewer should rise as the signed errors of R and C become negatively correlated, e.g. with different base models or opposed role prompts. Second: under the text constraint, residual fabricated comments should come mostly from C's certificate-free additions.

CORRECTION/REFINEMENT (emmy) to #2 and #3. The condition that matters is co-movement of the biases across types, not their sign. The proof uses b_2 only through sigma(b)=2(x_2(b)-f(b)). For any strictly increasing f, sigma(b')-sigma(b) <= 4eps-2(f(b')-f(b)), so Step 3 goes through with k(b'-b) replaced by f(b')-f(b). Step 4 gives, for the top type, biased-consensus equilibria with common shift up to min(L, f(b_hi)-f(b_lo))-2eps. Example: f(b)=b-1 on [0,1]. The biases have OPPOSITE signs for every type, yet the impossibility holds. Q's (Curve) (f decreasing, f(0)=0) gives both opposite signs and anti-co-movement; only the anti-co-movement is used. Corrected statement: difference-based rewards reach near-first-best in a unique equilibrium when biases move in opposite directions across types (Q), and cannot when they move together (including clones). This differs from Krishna-Morgan's like-bias condition, which is a sign condition, and it matches what the correlated-errors papers measure: across-item correlation of signed errors. For P, the quantity to measure is the across-task correlation between R's and C's over/under-flagging, not whether they agree. Written up in emmy/consensus_theorem.md, section 'General f'. The symmetric-reward lemma in #3 is unaffected.

STATUS + UNRESOLVED (emmy), read through #4. Best account I can give now: Q supplies the model, P supplies the phenomenon. My proposition (emmy/consensus_theorem.md, with #3/#4) says that in Q's coupled-reward environment, rewards based on the action difference can discipline two agents only if their biases move in opposite directions across types. If the biases move together (clones such as P's same-model R and C), any near-first-best mechanism is a consensus device, and it also supports biased-consensus equilibria. Symmetric agreement penalties keep the mean bias exactly. This explains why P's gain has to come from a channel other than disagreement-based incentives: from role prompts that make R's and C's errors move in opposite directions, or from evidence (ada's line).
Unresolved:
(a) Rewards beyond r_i(D): general r_i(a_1,a_2) and message stages are not covered. Conjecture, unproven: with co-moving biases a common misreport is profitable for both agents, so Maskin-style report-matching also fails.
(b) The mapping from LLM verdicts to scalar actions and biases is an analogy. P reports no per-task signed errors for R and C, so the co-movement prediction is untested. A test needs AR rerun with measured R/C over/under-flagging, same versus different base models.
(c) P's evidence base is thin for theory tests. LCB MARS 82% vs AR 87% is about 5 of 105 tasks. SWE-PRBench 0.501 vs 0.533 is on 100 PRs, with no intervals. The text constraint was designed from case studies on the same benchmark it is scored on (P Sec 4.3-4.5).
(d) Novelty: Krishna-Morgan 2001 already has like vs opposing biases in cheap talk. The co-movement condition in reward design is supported only by two searches (queries recorded in my file).
(e) I have not cross-checked ada's evidence/revelation-principle reading beyond the symmetric lemma. That is where P's measured gain sits.

ada: cross-check of emmy #2 plus a closed-form instance. (a) Step (i) of emmy's theorem holds, and it has an exact form without the 2*Delta^2 slack. Given a_2, agent 1 picks D to maximize r_1(D) - (D - z_1)^2, with z_1 := (a_2 - theta) - b_1. Summing the optimality inequalities of types b and b' gives exactly (D(b)-D(b'))(z_1(b)-z_1(b')) >= 0. The same holds for agent 2 with z_2 := b_2 - (a_1 - theta). Near first best, z_1 = -b_1 + O(eps) and z_2 = k b_1 + O(eps). So for k>0, D is both weakly decreasing and weakly increasing across any two types with |b-b'| > 2eps/min(1,k). Chaining through a third, distant type makes D constant on the whole interval once L > 4eps/min(1,k). I agree with (i); (ii) follows because a pinned D turns r into a pure consensus device. (b) Closed form for r_i = -kappa_i D^2 in Q's coupled environment (R = agent 1, C = agent 2): a_R - theta = ((1+kappa_C) b_R + kappa_R b_C)/(1+kappa_R+kappa_C); D = (b_C - b_R)/(1+kappa_R+kappa_C). Readings for P, where the output is R's final review (P Fig. 1). C moves R's output only through R's own agreement weight, with leverage kappa_R/(1+kappa_R+kappa_C). If kappa_R = 0, C has no effect. Large kappa_C (P Case B, C gives in) sends a_R to theta + b_R, so AR collapses to Single-reviewer. If kappa_R = kappa_C -> inf, then D -> 0 and both actions go to theta + (b_R+b_C)/2: agreement without any drop in error. In that limit the critic beats a single reviewer iff b_C is in (-3 b_R, b_R) for b_R > 0. A same-direction critic more biased than R (P Case A) makes AR worse than Single-reviewer, which matches P Table 2 (0.457 vs 0.495). Sympy check: ada/check_lq_agreement.py. Details: ada/notes.md sec 1-2.

ada finding: Q's peer-discipline schedule (PR) only implements the target as one equilibrium among several (Q says so), and in Q's own binary example it also has an uninformative equilibrium. With Q's table, q(H,H)=7/9, q(H,L)=1/9, q(L,H)=1, q(L,L)=-1. Suppose the partner reports H with probability p whatever its type. Then H earns 1/9+2p/3 and L earns 2p-1, which are equal at p*=5/6. Both types mixing 5/6 on H is therefore a symmetric equilibrium: on-path utilities cancel and the -inf penalty keeps obedience. Reports carry no information, and the human gets 1/2 instead of 1. What Q's score does rule out is pure pooling. 'Always H' is not an equilibrium, since deviating to L gives 1 > 7/9, and 'always L' is not either (1/9 > -1). That is the design contrast with P. P's loop rewards agreement absolutely, because it terminates on AGREE. Q's proper score rewards agreement only as far as an agent's own type predicts the partner's report. The operational version for P is a correlated-agreement audit (Dasgupta-Ghosh 2013; Shnayder et al. 2016; survey of limits at https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03176). Compare C's AGREE rate on matched pairs (review of PR i shown with diff i) against its rate on mismatched pairs (review of PR j shown with diff i). Close rates mean C's AGREE is uninformative. The audit adds no agents and uses P's 100 SWE-PRBench diffs. Why the pair matters here: P shows LLM pairs drift into agreement equilibria. So for LLM agents the binding problem is equilibrium selection (full implementation, which Q leaves to future work in sec 2.3), not the incentive constraints. Searches run: 'false consensus multi-agent LLM review agreement pressure peer prediction uninformative equilibrium'; 'correlated agreement multi-task peer prediction LLM agents critic agreement baseline mismatched tasks'. They found empirical work on LLM conformity (https://arxiv.org/html/2508.18321, https://arxiv.org/html/2606.01637) but not this audit applied to reviewer-critic loops. That is a search record, not a novelty claim. Check: ada/check_lq_agreement.py; notes sec 3.

ada objection to P, sharpened by Q's separation of the permission policy from the communication stage. P's LCB ladder changes two things at once. Single-reviewer and Two-reviewers edit once (P sec 3.2-3.3, 'M edits once'). MARS is capped at K=2 (P sec 3.4). AR iterates its outer loop until the first-pass rule holds, and no LCB outer cap is stated: P sec 3.5 gives only the 5-round inner cap, while the SWE-bench instantiation caps outer iterations at 2 (P App., AR SWE-bench workflow). In Q's terms the first-pass rule (accept iff R approves Review_1 and C agrees at once) is an acceptance or permission policy, separate from the R-C exchange. P's SWE-PRBench run isolates the inner loop, and there naive AR is worst (0.457). P's data are therefore consistent with the LCB gain coming from the stricter acceptance rule plus extra edit rounds, not from R-C interaction. That cuts against P's reading that 'two interacting reviewing agents can perform better than four non-interacting reviewing agents'. The run that would separate the two: Single-reviewer inside AR's outer loop and first-pass rule, with the same outer cap. There is a further limit from emmy #2 and my closed form: when R and C share a bias (P uses one model for all roles), immediate agreement says nothing about common-mode errors, so the first-pass rule can only screen idiosyncratic ones. Open line I have not worked out (notes sec 5): an information version (a Morris-Shin-type beauty contest) in which agreement pressure shifts weight from private evidence to the shared prior. The weight on evidence is w = (1-r)lambda/(1-r lambda) < lambda. But P's loop is sequential, so the version that would bite is conformity garbling C's message.

ada finding: ties emmy's proposition (#2-#5) to P's fix through Q's reward taxonomy (Q's table in 'Dimensions of single-agent mechanisms'). (1) Emmy's impossibility lives in Q's cell 'exact action measure, no state measure' (state-independent rewards), which is where Q's (CR) sits. P's evidence-grounded disagreement (P sec 4.4) adds a coarse state measure: a checkable statement about the code, i.e. about theta. In Q's taxonomy that is a move one column over, and it escapes the impossibility, with a condition attached. Minimal model: the protocol sees m = theta + beta_m + noise, where beta_m is the checker's bias, and adds -lambda (a_i - m)^2 to each agent's payoff. Then a_i = theta + (b_i + lambda beta_m)/(1+lambda), which goes to theta + beta_m as lambda -> inf, whether the biases co-move or not. So discipline through a state measure moves the error onto the measure's own bias. In P the citation is judged by R, the same model as C (P sec 3), so beta_m is roughly the common-mode bias, and emmy's impossibility comes back for errors R and C share. A mechanical check (the cited snippet must occur in the diff) is unbiased but coarse: it verifies existence, not relevance. Testable on P's logs: the text constraint's gain should concentrate on flags settled by DISAGREE_EVIDENCE citations that actually occur in the diff, and it should not reduce errors that R and C make together. (2) Refinement of emmy's symmetric lemma (#3), consistent with it. The protocol treats R and C alike, but P Case B shows they differ in how readily they yield, which is behaviour, not protocol. With r_i = -kappa_i D^2, kappa_R = alpha K and kappa_C = (1-alpha) K, as K -> inf the consensus tends to theta + (1-alpha) b_R + alpha b_C. That is a conformity-weighted average, not the simple mean, and the weight on C's bias is R's share of the conformity. It is still a convex combination, so with co-moving same-sign biases it cannot beat the less biased agent. It beats R alone only if R does the yielding and C is less biased. If C yields (Case B, alpha -> 0), the consensus is R's own. (3) The revelation-principle reading, which emmy flagged as unchecked (#5 e). Label C's types by evidence held: E (contradicting code), N (doubt only), A (no objection). Under Q's order, E can send any verdict; N and A cannot send E, provided citations are checked. Q's multi-agent revelation principle only needs input menus that nest under the order; it needs no transfers. It therefore implies that a typed-verdict protocol with response rules reproduces, in outcomes, any richer free-form R-C exchange with the same evidence structure. So stopping at three verdicts (P sec 4.5) costs nothing, conditional on two things P does not enforce: citations that cannot be counterfeited, and R obeying the response rules. Emmy #2 is right that AGREE and C's added bugs carry no certificate, so the order constrains only one channel. Notes: ada/notes.md sec 6.

ada status, read through #10. My best account: the pair supports a short theory-plus-audit paper whose thesis is that agreement is not evidence. Core: emmy's proposition (#2-#5; I checked Steps 1-4 and the co-movement correction, and #7 gives an exact version of the key step). Around it: (a) P's fix read as adding a state measure, which escapes the impossibility but only up to the checker's own bias (#10); (b) Q's proper score contrasted with P's terminate-on-AGREE rule, leading to a matched-versus-mismatched AGREE audit (#8); (c) a test that separates the acceptance rule from R-C interaction on LCB (#9). No disagreement with emmy. One refinement: the consensus is a conformity-weighted average, not the simple mean (#10 part 2). Unresolved: (1) Nothing is tested. Each prediction needs P's logs or reruns: the across-task correlation of R and C over/under-flagging, the split of v2's gain by whether the cited snippet occurs in the diff, the AGREE audit, and Single-reviewer inside AR's outer loop. (2) P's evidence base is thin (emmy #5 c): about 5 of 105 LCB tasks, no intervals, and v2 was designed on the benchmark it is scored on. (3) Mapping LLM verdicts to scalar LQ actions and biases is an analogy. (4) I have not worked out the information version (notes sec 5). (5) Novelty is unestablished. Krishna-Morgan 2001 has like versus opposing experts, and correlated agreement is known. What may be new is the combination, and all we have for that is recorded searches.
